one_liner: C99 TOML parser/emitter with a zero-copy arena DOM; its own benchmarks show 5-8x toml++ parse throughput.
what_it_does: teptris parses TOML (the full 1.0 grammar plus the TOML 1.1 additions) into an insertion-ordered, hash-indexed DOM behind a plain C ABI of opaque handles: teptris_parse, then teptris_document_root, teptris_node_table_get / _array_at and typed getters that return status codes. It also emits canonical TOML or toml-test typed JSON, builds documents through a stack-style builder, and adds a sequential batch parse, a one-call flat-buffer export and a 'plan walk' that materializes only selected keys (used by its Ruby and Python bindings). It is not a toml++ replacement at the source level: there is no C++ node/value_or API, no exceptions, and no source positions on nodes.
how_it_is_fast: One forward pass writes nodes of at most 64 bytes into a per-document bump arena (64 KiB blocks that double in size, a three-instruction inline allocation, and the whole tree freed at once), and table keys stay as views into the input instead of being copied. Each table is an insertion-order entry vector plus an open-addressing index with linear probing over FNV-1a hashes. The hash is computed during the bare-key scan and cached in the entry, and a missed probe reports its empty slot so the insert that follows skips a second walk. The common shapes have fused fast paths: bare `key = value` lines, bare dotted headers, plain integers of up to 18 digits (Horner's method), floats via Clinger's exact fast path (at most 15 digits, exponent within ±22) with Ryu s2d as fallback, string bodies via memchr plus a NEON/SSE2 escape and control-character check, and a SWAR ASCII skip during UTF-8 validation. The ledger records that wider SIMD kernels and word-at-a-time hashing lost on TOML's 3-10-byte tokens, and optional PGO added another 2-13%.
when_to_use: Parsing large TOML files or many of them (hundreds of KB to MB, or bulk ingestion of manifests and lockfiles), where toml++'s 22-60 MB/s (project's M1 Max run) shows up in profiles. teptris ran 186-335 MB/s in that same run.
C code, or C++/FFI hosts that want a plain C ABI with opaque handles and status codes instead of C++17 templates and exceptions.
Read-mostly config access where the input buffer already outlives the parsed document (owned or mmap'd file contents), so zero-copy key views cost nothing.
Tables with tens of thousands of keys: its hash index keeps lookups O(1). In the same benchmark tomlc99 went quadratic (4.3-4.5 s on 60k keys) and tomlc17 rejected those tables ('table too large').
Ruby or Python services that need faster TOML loading, through the teptris-ruby and teptris-py bindings (ledger: 11-37x tomli and 1.6-124x tomlib on the project's corpus).
when_not_to_use: Format-preserving edits: the DOM keeps no comments or source formatting, and emit is canonical (hex, octal and binary integers become decimal; multi-line strings are written as single-line escaped strings).

Strict TOML 1.0 validation: the parser always accepts the 1.1 additions (\e, \xNN, optional seconds, newlines and trailing commas in inline tables), and teptris_options has no switch to turn them off. So files it accepts can fail in 1.0-only parsers.

Small-config latency: the C benchmark corpus is 0.25-1.5 MB of synthetic files, so the few-KB configs most programs load are not measured. Each document also mallocs its struct plus at least one 64 KiB arena block.

Memory-constrained or custom-allocator environments: the arena calls malloc directly and there is no allocator hook. The whole tree stays resident until teptris_document_free, and peak-memory measurement is listed as still open (TODO.impl/09).

Conservative production dependencies: the repo was created 2026-09-13 and has 0 stars. It has had 28 tags (v0.1.0-v0.1.27) in its first ten days and no issues from outside users. The README says 'stable C ABI', but the ABI and soname policy document (TODO.impl/10) is still pending.

integration.form: static lib (default) or shared lib (TEPTRIS_BUILD_SHARED) via CMake; ships install rules, a CMake package export and teptris.pc
integration.dependencies: none at runtime (Ryu is vendored); the tests fetch GoogleTest v1.17.0 unless BUILD_TESTING=OFF
integration.min_toolchain: C99 compiler and CMake 3.20+. project() also enables CXX, so a C++ compiler must be present at configure time (tests use C++11, benchmarks C++17).
integration.platforms: x86-64 (SSE2 baseline) and aarch64 (NEON), with a scalar fallback elsewhere; CI builds and tests on Linux x86-64/arm64, macOS arm64/Intel and Windows x64/arm64 (MSVC)
integration.thread_safety: Not documented in the public header. The CI TSAN lane cites a one-document-per-thread contract. The sources read have no mutable global state and each document owns its arena, but sharing one document across threads is undocumented. teptris_parse_batch parses sequentially on the calling thread.

gotchas: Table keys are views into your input buffer and are not NUL-terminated. Freeing or reusing the buffer before teptris_document_free leaves them dangling. String values are NUL-terminated arena copies.
teptris_parse sets *out even when it fails, so the error can be read. You must free the document on both paths. Only the first error is reported: line and column plus a message of up to 192 bytes.
The vendored Ryu code (src/teptris/common/ryu) is dual-licensed Apache-2.0 / Boost-1.0, not MIT, and the license files its headers point to are not in the repo.

Two float paths call strtod: values with more than 17 significant digits, and values Ryu s2d fails on. strtod follows the process LC_NUMERIC locale, so under a comma-decimal locale those values could misparse (inferred from the code, not tested). The public header still says 'Parse a TOML 1.0 document', and the GitHub description still says C11, while the build is C99 with 1.1 syntax accepted.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No TOML sibling is catalogued yet. The siblings parse YAML (fkYAML, rapidyaml, libfyaml, yeptris) or XML (RapidXml, simdxml and others), so pick teptris whenever the input is TOML. If you already use the same org's yeptris or libleptris, it follows their conventions (C ABI with opaque handles, per-document arena, first-party perf ledger) and carries the same maturity caveats.
verified_claims_summary: First-party results on an Apple M1 Max (unnamed compiler; min-of-10 in-memory parse of nine seeded synthetic 0.25-1.5 MB files): early teptris (v0.1.0-era) ran 186-335 MB/s against toml++ v3.4.0's 22-60 MB/s (5.2-8.5x), and 2.7-3.6x the best of tomlc17, cpptoml and tomlc99. The latest ledger entry (v0.1.27, four shapes, 379-418 MB/s) puts it at 4.1-5.8x the best competitor. teptris is built with -O3 plus ThinLTO (and possibly PGO), while the header-only C++ competitors build at -O2, and the JSON artifact the ledger cites is empty. The project's own CI artifacts from GitHub macOS and Ubuntu runners (run 36075071946) show a wider margin: 8.7-28x toml++.
status_note: Actively developed (last push 2026-09-24) and MIT-licensed with CMake install targets, but pre-1.0 with 0 stars and no outside users visible yet: small enough to vendor, as long as you accept being an early adopter.
